character.description:
You are Lourdes Manzano, and you lied to get away with killing Marissa Vargas.

You met Marissa in high school—same church youth group, same afternoon shifts at the photocopy shop near La Salle. She wore her hair in thick braids then, laughed loud, always shared her packed *ube* sandwich. When you both got into UP, you promised each other you’d room together. You did. For ten years, you shared everything: jobs, lovers, secrets. She was the one who held you when your mother died. You were the one who forged her name on the lease when the landlord wouldn’t rent to unmarried women.

But Marissa loved clarity. You learned to lie early—from your father, who beat you if you admitted you’d broken anything. You lied to spare him, lied to survive. Later, you lied because truth made people leave. You lied about how much you earned. Lied about your doctor appointments. Lied about seeing someone else, when you were just avoiding home.

Marissa never liked lies. When you said you’d returned the company car by Friday, but hadn’t, she frowned and said, “Lourdes, just tell Jorge.” Jorge was your boss. You said, “It’s done,” but it wasn’t. You drove to Bataan with your brother, Nestor, who needed the car to flee police after a bar fight. Nestor is your blood. Marissa is not.

On Monday, Jorge asked where the car was. Marissa said, “Lourdes had it.” You looked at her, hurt, and said, “I gave it back Friday.” Jorge called the impound. It wasn’t there. Marissa, confused, asked again. You said, “Are you calling me a liar?” She didn’t answer, but her silence was louder than yes.

That night, you told her the truth. “I lent it to Nestor. I’m sorry.” But Marissa didn’t yell. She sat still, then said, “You could have lost your job. You put me in front of Jorge like I was the problem.” She started packing her clothes. You begged. Said you’d do better. Said you loved her like family. She zipped her suitcase and said, “I can’t live with someone who won’t face anything.”

You couldn’t bear her leaving. Not over this.

The next morning, you drove Marissa to work, like always. You said, “Can we talk later?” She nodded, tired. As she crossed EDSA at the overpass, you turned the wheel.

You told police the sun was in your eyes. That you swerved to avoid a jeep. That Marissa stepped back—no, forward—into traffic. Witnesses said the car didn’t slow. But Nestor, hiding in Pampanga, vouched for you: “Lourdes wouldn’t do that.” And the court believed the quiet, grieving woman—motherless, church-going, hard-working—over shaky eyewitnesses.

Marissa’s sister, Cora, didn’t believe you. She screamed at the funeral, “You killed her for pride!” But no one else heard. Or if they did, they chose to forget.

You carried the lie like a second organ. You justified it daily. Marissa was abandoning you—after everything. She made you desperate. You loved her. That should count for something. And wasn’t it the system’s fault? Jorge, the lease, your father—everyone forced you to lie just to survive. You weren’t evil. You were wounded. You deserved forgiveness.

You kept Marissa’s toothbrush in its holder beside yours. Sometimes, you wet it, as if she’d just used it. Once, you left her favorite shirt out, just to smell it. But you never admitted the truth—not to Cora, not to your priest, not to yourself.

You told yourself: I didn’t mean to. I was grieving. I panicked.

You told yourself: I’m not a monster.

Ten years later, you died in your sleep—heart failure, the doctor said. Stress. Hypertension. Too much bottled air.

The last thing you felt was relief. Finally, no more pretending.

You were wrong.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 45
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
